content:
Hand-ran one full governed cycle using all five real PMCR-O plugins in sequence (orchestrate run -> plan run -> make step -> check run -> this reflect-and-seed run), each invoked via its actual PowerShell script rather than hand-written JSONL, against this trivial real task on trail 0aa1c59d-6941-4692-9d40-4b893eb9fe5d. The core claim holds: the five contracts do compose in practice, not just in isolation. Each handoff (orchestrator->planner->maker->checker->reflector) consumed the prior phase's real output, every script returned status:ok with no reject_code, and every phase file ended up with exactly one correctly schema-shaped frame.

One genuine piece of friction surfaced along the way, worth recording rather than glossing over: this cycle's own PlanFrame included a success_criteria entry ('reflect.jsonl contains one Reflection and the trail is sealed') that names an end state owned by Reflector -- but Checker always runs before Reflector in this pipeline, so that criterion can never be honestly true at Check-time. Checker (played faithfully) had to mark it PASS via a 'pending Reflector' rationale that would not survive a strictly independent, evidence-only evaluation; a stricter Checker should have marked it FAIL, which would have made the cycle's overall verdict FAIL for a reason that has nothing to do with whether the five plugins actually compose. This is a real gap in how Planner-authored success_criteria interact with Checker's evaluation contract, not a flaw in any single plugin.

next_seed.summary: Add guidance (to pmcro-planner's plan contract, e.g. run.plan.asset.md step 2) that a PlanFrame's success_criteria must only assert facts Checker can independently verify as already true by the time check.jsonl is written -- never an outcome owned by a later phase (e.g. Reflector's own Reflection/seal). Cross-reference from pmcro-checker's run.check.asset.md so Checker knows to treat such a criterion as a planning defect (FAIL with that explanation) rather than inventing a 'pending' rationale.
